name: Seville
title: Seville River Port UTM | Ship Thickness Gauging Guadalquivir
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in the Port of Seville for coasters, bulk, project cargo and river-going ships: hold frames, tanks, decks and pre-docking readings.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging on the Guadalquivir: The Port of Seville
intro: Seville is Spain's only major inland sea port, far up the Guadalquivir and reached by a long, pilot-led river passage and a sea lock. Coasters, bulk and project-cargo ships work quays that sit among the city's industry, and repairs there tend to be done afloat. Technicians travel from India to the ship for ultrasonic gauging, planned around the river transit, the lock and the cargo programme.

highlights.h: A sea port behind a lock
highlights.p: Ships reach Seville through a pilotage passage up the Guadalquivir and through a lock. Timing is controlled and fixed, so gauging plans are built around the confirmed arrival and departure windows.
Once inside the lock, ships lie in still water with no ocean swell. That makes alongside gauging comfortable and predictable compared with open Atlantic ports on the same coast.
Conventional cargo, fertiliser and grain bulk, and heavy project loads such as wind equipment keep the quays busy. We gauge holds, decks and tank boundaries between cargo operations.

port.h: Seville: an inland sea port on the Guadalquivir
p: The port of Seville lies a long way upstream from the river mouth at Sanlúcar de Barrameda. Ships make the passage under compulsory pilotage, with draught and tide controlling how deep a ship may come, and then enter the port area through a lock that separates the tidal river from the dock basin. The Autoridad Portuaria de Sevilla manages the quays, which include a dock basin and berths along the river, set among industrial land south of the city.

Cargo is mixed and mostly short-sea. Coasters and general cargo ships bring and take steel, machinery and agricultural products. Bulk carriers handle grain, fertiliser and other dry cargoes, and project cargo such as wind-turbine components, heavy plant and industrial equipment is a regular speciality. Small tankers and bunker craft work the liquid trades, and river and coastal cruise craft occasionally visit. Ships rarely exceed the size the river and lock can handle, so the fleet is dominated by handy, small and medium vessels.

For inspection, the setting has two consequences. The passage and lock make a call to Seville a planned operation, so owners tend to combine cargo work with maintenance and survey tasks while the ship is there. And ships that use the river repeatedly meet silt, mud and brackish water, which can accelerate wear on shell plating, sea chests and ballast tanks that take river water. Gauging gives owners a clear view of structure before the next survey or a docking at a yard on the Atlantic coast.

facilities.h: Where gauging fits in the Port of Seville
p: Nearly all gauging is done alongside at the cargo quays and lay-by berths inside the lock. General cargo and bulk ships can be gauged between discharge and loading, with hold frames, tank tops, coamings and hatch cover structure readily accessible in calm water. Project-cargo ships, which often have long stays for heavy lifts, offer extended windows for deck and ballast tank work. Ships lying idle or waiting for cargo at lay-by berths allow longer programmes with fewer interruptions from cargo operations.

The port has ship-repair capacity on the river for smaller commercial ships, tugs and workboats, but larger ships needing a drydock typically go to yards on the Atlantic coast, with Cádiz bay the closest major centre. Anchorage work does not apply here because ships do not wait on the river as they would off an open coast; any pre-arrival gauging is done at the previous port. Technicians can follow the ship to the repair yard for post-blast readings if the owner wants them, and the steel list from Seville serves as the starting point.
list: General cargo and bulk quays: hold frame, tank top, coaming and hatch cover gauging between discharge and loading
Project-cargo berths: deck, ballast tank and hull plating readings during long stays for heavy-lift work
Lay-by berths inside the lock: coasters and cargo ships waiting for employment or a yard slot
River-side repair quays: smaller ships, tugs and workboats under repair afloat or on slipways
Liquid-bulk berths: deck and ballast tank gauging on small tankers and bunker craft, subject to terminal rules
Yards in Cádiz bay and along the Atlantic coast: docking-stage gauging after steel lists are prepared in Seville

context.h: River navigation, regulation and the local trade
p: Port state control at Seville is exercised for the Paris MoU by inspectors of the Capitanía Marítima under the Dirección General de la Marina Mercante. Small cargo ships on regional trades are frequent subjects, and inspectors check structure, hatch covers and watertight integrity closely. Because ships in Seville have made a river transit and a lock passage, their records of draught and ballast handling matter to the master, and a recent set of readings supports any discussion about structure or damage from groundings or contact with the bank.

EU rules add pressure on older coasters and bulkers. The Ship Recycling Regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on ships calling at EU ports, and owners deciding whether to renew or retire ageing tonnage commonly review structure at the same time. EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime also affect operating decisions on short-sea ships. Gauging in a calm, controlled port like Seville produces clear, repeatable measurements that owners can use in those decisions.

jobs.h: Gauging jobs we see at Seville
jobs.p: Requests tend to come from owners of coasters, bulk carriers and project-cargo ships who want evidence before a survey, a sale or a docking, and who have a known stay alongside. Because the lock and river passage fix the schedule, planning is straightforward once dates are confirmed. The team travels from India with portable gauges and magnetic particle equipment. Typical jobs include:
list: Hold frame and tank top gauging on a handy bulk carrier unloading grain, with readings compared against the diminution limits for its survey.
Hatch cover, coaming and deck plating gauging on a project-cargo ship during a long stay for heavy-lift loading, with magnetic particle testing at coaming corners.
Sea chest and bottom shell readings on a coaster after repeated river passages, supporting a steel estimate for a docking on the coast.
Ballast tank and double-bottom gauging on a general cargo ship lying idle at a lay-by berth while waiting for employment.
Pre-purchase condition gauging of an older coaster at the cargo quay, covering holds, tanks and main deck for a buyer's superintendent.

logistics: Technicians fly from India through a European hub to Seville Airport, which is close to the city, and reach the port by road. The ship's agent arranges port and lock access and informs the team of the river passage schedule. Indian nationals need a Schengen visa to enter Spain, so travel is timed around visa issue and the ship's confirmed arrival, and since river passages are scheduled in advance, dates are usually firm enough to plan with confidence.

faqs.q: Is Seville a practical place to gauge a ship given the river passage?
faqs.a: Yes, because the passage and the lock make arrival dates predictable and the quays are calm. The ship's agent confirms the transit schedule, we plan technician travel against it, and gauging proceeds alongside once the ship has berthed. Longer stays for heavy-lift or waiting for cargo give the most room for a full programme.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Seville for steel renewal?
faqs.a: The port has repair capacity on the river for smaller vessels, but larger ships usually dock at yards on the Atlantic coast, with the Bay of Cádiz the nearest major centre. Gauging in Seville gives the yard a steel list in advance, and technicians can attend the dock for post-blast readings.

faqs.q: Does river water affect hull condition?
faqs.a: It can. Silt, mud and brackish water accelerate wear in sea chests, shell plating near the waterline and ballast tanks that take river water. We gauge those areas on a grid and compare readings with earlier survey figures, so the owner can see whether wear is general or concentrated and plan maintenance accordingly.

faqs.q: Can project-cargo ships be gauged during heavy-lift operations?
faqs.a: Yes, in areas not affected by the lift. Deck plating away from the working area, ballast tanks and hold structure can usually be gauged while loading proceeds, with permits arranged by the ship. We agree the exclusion zones with the chief officer and the lift supervisor beforehand so the work stays safe.

faqs.q: How far ahead should a request for gauging at Seville be made?
faqs.a: As early as the call is planned. Schengen visas need time, and river passages are fixed in advance, so confirmed dates normally come well before arrival. Short-notice requests are still worth sending with the berth, dates and scope, and we will say honestly whether a team can reach the ship in time.
